content: The World Health Organization (WHO) Steering Group conducted a scoping review in 2015 to evaluate interventions aimed at reducing caesarean section rates. This review included systematic searches across six electronic databases (Cochrane Library, PubMed, Embase, LILACS, CINAHL, and EBSCO) and identified 11 relevant systematic reviews published between 2001 and January 2016. These reviews encompassed findings from 99 unique studies conducted in 32 countries, predominantly high-income nations. The studies examined 151 intervention components, with 21 distinct components grouped into four main domains: education, labor management, regulatory/administrative measures, and other strategies. In April 2016, the Steering Group convened a meeting in Geneva, Switzerland, to identify priority questions and define the scope of guidelines. These questions were categorized into background and foreground questions. Background questions provided contextual information for recommendations, such as the global prevalence and trends of caesarean delivery, the definition of unnecessary caesarean sections, the contribution of healthy women to overall caesarean rates, and the complications and burdens associated with unnecessary caesareans. Foreground questions guided the evidence review process to inform recommendations. The population of interest for these guidelines included women seeking antenatal, labor, and delivery care, their families, healthcare professionals (midwives, nurses, and physicians), maternity care facilities, and communities or advocacy groups involved in maternity care. The scoping and consultation process identified 12 key questions and priority outcomes. In 2015, WHO released a statement indicating that caesarean rates above 10% at the population level were not associated with reductions in maternal and newborn mortality. The statement emphasized that this threshold should not be applied at the hospital level due to variations in obstetric case mix. Furthermore, the statement did not recommend an ideal caesarean rate due to insufficient evidence on the effects of caesareans on maternal, perinatal, and neonatal morbidity, as well as psychological and social well-being. The guideline development process focused on non-clinical interventions to reduce unnecessary caesareans. Preparatory work was organized into three streams: updating Cochrane reviews on the effectiveness and safety of non-clinical interventions, synthesizing qualitative evidence on barriers and facilitators to intervention use, and analyzing implementation considerations. Evidence was derived from randomized controlled trials (RCTs), non-randomized controlled trials (nRCTs), controlled before-and-after studies, interrupted time series studies, and cohort studies. The quality of evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach, which considers factors such as risk of bias, study limitations, consistency, and precision of results. Qualitative evidence was synthesized to explore the views and experiences of women, healthcare professionals, and organizations regarding non-clinical interventions. This included factors influencing the success or failure of interventions, as well as their impact on decision-making and preferences. Implementation-related factors, such as organizational culture, staffing interventions, and financial strategies, were also examined. The WHO guideline methodology included a rigorous assessment of the risk of bias in included studies, using tools such as the Cochrane EPOC criteria and the ROBINS-I tool for non-randomized studies. The certainty of evidence was rated as high, moderate, low, or very low, based on predefined criteria. Results were presented narratively due to heterogeneity in study designs and interventions. In summary, the WHO guidelines aim to provide evidence-based recommendations for non-clinical interventions to reduce unnecessary caesarean sections, addressing barriers, facilitators, and implementation considerations to ensure effective adoption and scale-up of proven strategies.
